name: Biscay Green
lede: Biscay Green is a muted yellow-green from Ridgway's 1912 systematic nomenclature, measured so close to the library's own Moss that the two sit about three units apart.

sections.title: A Ridgway hue, later folded into ISCC-NBS
sections.body:
Robert Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* (1912) places Biscay Green on plate XVII, hue 27′, tone i [1]. A second, very close entry sits on plate XXXI, hue 29′′, also tone i [1]. The National Bureau of Standards folded both into its 1955 ISCC-NBS system as block 120, *moderate yellow green*, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary is cited for the same block by the 1955 circular [1]. Ridgway's own plates give no account of why he chose the name Biscay, and none is documented here [1].

The library's measurements put this swatch almost on top of [[moss|Moss]], about 3.3 units off, and it also sits near a second Ridgway and ISCC-NBS entry that our data groups as a near-duplicate, within about 2.3 units [2]. The painted hue most associated with the same shade cluster is [[roman-green|Roman Green]], which turns up on the same canvases more often than chance [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color match to this swatch in 361 of 23,781 paintings, 1.52 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 187, more common than 69 percent of the named colors we track [3]. Georges Seurat is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 8 of the 41 [[painter:georges-seurat|Seurat]] paintings in the archive, 8.9 times the rate expected from the museums his works come from [3].

Usage peaks in the 1900s, with 35 of 1,674 paintings from that decade carrying it, 2.4 times the expected rate, and inside a painting it most often plays an accent (39 percent of its 187 within-painting matches) [3]. The earliest match dates to 916, nearly a thousand years before the name's 1912 record, which shows only that a similar-looking hue existed in paint long before the word did, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. India is the most over-represented country, at 2.1 times its expected share, and the color shares canvases with Roman Green far more than chance would predict [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [3].
